Abstract
The industrial manufacturing of chemicals consumes a significant amount of energy and raw
materials. In principle, the development of new catalysts could greatly improve the efficiency of
chemical production. However, the discovery of viable catalysts can be exceedingly challenging
because it is difficult to know the efficacy of a candidate without experimentally synthesizing and
characterizing it. This study explores the feasibility of using fault-tolerant quantum computers to
accelerate the discovery of homogeneous catalysts for nitrogen fixation, an industrially important
chemical process. It introduces a set of ground-state energy estimation problems representative
of calculations needed for the discovery of homogeneous catalysts and analyzes them on three
dimensions: economic utility, classical hardness, and quantum resource requirements.

methods.value: The study introduces a set of ground-state energy estimation problems representative of calculations needed for the discovery of homogeneous catalysts and analyzes them on three dimensions: economic utility, classical hardness, and quantum resource requirements.

problems.value: The industrial manufacturing of chemicals consumes a significant amount of energy and raw materials, and the discovery of viable catalysts can greatly improve the efficiency of chemical production but is challenging due to the difficulty in knowing the efficacy of a candidate without experimentally synthesizing and characterizing it.

hypotheses.value: Using fault-tolerant quantum computers can accelerate the discovery of homogeneous catalysts for nitrogen fixation, an industrially important chemical process.

evidence.value: The economic utility of running these computations is estimated to be $200,000 for the highest utility problem considered, and the required runtime for double-factorized phase estimation on a fault-tolerant superconducting device is estimated to be 139,000 QPU-hours under conservative assumptions.

conclusions.value: With continued development, it will be feasible for fault-tolerant quantum computers to accelerate the discovery of homogeneous catalysts.
